title: Reading Glasses or Just Tired Eyes?

patient.name: Mr Chua Boon Huat
patient.presenting_complaint: Difficulty reading small print on documents and his phone over the past year

history.hpc: Mr Chua reports increasing difficulty reading fine print on financial statements and his mobile phone over the past 12 months. He finds himself holding documents further away to read them clearly. He has not previously worn glasses for reading. His distance vision is unaffected — he drives without glasses with no issues. He is here for a routine check after his optician suggested he see an eye doctor before getting reading glasses.
history.pmhx: No known eye conditions. No diabetes. No hypertension.
history.social_hx: Works in an office, spends most of the day reading documents and using a computer and phone. Non-smoker.

examination_findings.anterior_segment: Not assessed at this stage — PSA role is vision testing only

near_va.method: Near Vision (N) chart held at 35cm in adequate lighting, each eye tested separately with the other occluded, then both eyes together, no near correction worn

diagnosis: Distance VA normal (6/6 both eyes). Near VA reduced to N12 unaided at age 51, consistent with age-related reduction in near focusing ability. Results recorded for doctor review — PSA does not diagnose presbyopia.

immediate: Confirm patient identity and explain that, as this is part of his routine visit, both distance and near vision will be checked
Perform hand hygiene and wipe the occluder and N chart holder with alcohol wipes
First confirm distance VA has been completed (6/6 both eyes unaided)
Explain the near vision test: 'I will hold this card at about an arm's length from your eyes — please read the smallest print you can manage comfortably'
Hold the N chart at the standard 35cm distance in a well-lit area
Test the right eye first, occluding the left eye, and record the smallest line read comfortably
Repeat for the left eye, occluding the right eye
Test both eyes together (binocular near vision) and record the result
Wipe the chart and occluder with alcohol wipes and perform hand hygiene after the test
follow_up: Record all near vision results (right, left, and binocular) in N-notation in SCM alongside the distance VA results
Hand the completed results to the doctor for review
Note in the form that the patient reports symptoms consistent with near-vision difficulty for the doctor's information
patient_education: Inform Mr Chua that both his distance and near vision tests are complete and the doctor will review the results
If he asks whether he needs reading glasses, explain that the doctor will discuss this with him after reviewing all the findings
Reassure him that difficulty with near vision in his age group is a common reason patients visit the eye clinic, without naming a specific diagnosis

key_points: Confirms patient identity and the purpose of the visit
Notes the symptom pattern (near vision difficulty, normal distance vision) accurately
Confirms patient is not currently wearing any reading correction before testing unaided near vision
Records relevant occupational context (reading-intensive work) without speculating on diagnosis
Uses the N chart at the correct 35cm testing distance with adequate lighting
Tests each eye separately with correct occlusion before testing both eyes together
Records results using correct N-notation (e.g., N12, N10)
Performs hand hygiene and wipes equipment before and after the test
Ensures distance VA has also been completed as part of the routine check
Recognises that reduced near vision with normal distance vision in a 51-year-old is a common, expected pattern but does not name presbyopia to the patient
Does not tell the patient he needs reading glasses or a specific add power
Documents both distance and near results together for the doctor's full picture
Defers all interpretation and prescribing decisions to the doctor
Communicates the test process clearly and sets expectations for next steps
Documents results accurately and completely in the correct notation
Avoids giving the patient any diagnosis or treatment recommendation
Maintains a professional, reassuring manner appropriate for a routine check
